full-data.t: We have **ten houses with known prices**. If we judged a model on the same houses it learned from, it would always look good, so we split them into **separate roles**.

split.t: **Five** houses to train on, **three** to validate and **two** for the test set. The test houses go into a **locked drawer**; nobody looks at them yet.

train-models.t: Two candidates: a **flat model** (always the average price) and a **straight line**. Their parameters are learned from the **five training houses only**.

training-results.t: On the training houses the flat model has **MSE 1.2024** and the line **0.0166**. Training error alone would rank models by how flexible they are, so it **cannot choose**.

validation-results.t: Now score each model on the **three validation houses** it has never seen: flat **2.5629**, line **0.0111**. The residuals on these houses are the **honest signal**.

compare.t: **Lower validation MSE is better.** The line is far better than the flat model. Choosing among models, and tuning hyperparameters like the polynomial degree or λ, is the **validation set's job**.

choose-model.t: We pick the straight line. Its **parameters came from the training set**; our **choice came from the validation set**. (The overfit curve of the earlier lesson, with validation 3.0073, would have lost too.)

test-stays-locked.t: The test houses were **never used to fit or to choose**. They are scored once, at the very end. Using validation for many choices makes its score slightly optimistic, which is why the test set must **stay untouched**.
